title: Armed Naxals wiped out, must identify, defeat 'dimagi' Naxals: PM in Bastar
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Express News Service)
syllabus: GS3 › Linkages between development and spread of extremism; role of external state and non-state actors in internal security · GS3 › Security forces and agencies and their mandate · GS2 › Welfare of vulnerable sections (tribal areas) · GS4 › Inclusive and good governance
summary: Celebrating Diwali with the CRPF in Bastar, the PM said armed Naxalites have vanished from the forests but 'intellectual' Naxals remain; only seven districts were categorised as LWE-affected in a February 2026 review.
evolution: MHA review: only seven districts (five in Chhattisgarh, one each in Jharkhand and Odisha) categorised as LWE-affected.
Home Minister tells the Lok Sabha the country has become 'Naxal-free', against a March 31 target.
PM in Bastar: first Diwali 'when every district of the country is free from Naxalism'.
ideas: LWE districts: ~200 (early 2000s) → 7 (Feb 2026).
GS3 · LWE
Sustained action can roll back insurgency.
Two-pronged strategy: firm operations plus roads, towers, schools.
GS3 · Development and extremism
Security clears; development holds.
Restoring the state: free movement and the right to vote return.
GS2 · Grassroots democracy
Security is a precondition for democracy.
Next battle is of ideas: win trust, protect dissent.
GS3 · Ideology / GS4
Territory is won by force; trust by governance.
keywords: Clear, hold, build
Clearing an area of insurgents, holding it with forces, then building roads, schools and services
GS3 · Counter-insurgency
LWE's decline follows clear, hold, build: security first, then roads, towers and schools to hold the gains.
Governance deficit
The absence of state services that extremists exploit
GS3 · Development and extremism
LWE grew where the state was absent; filling the governance deficit is the lasting cure.
Urban Naxalism
Sympathy or support for LWE ideology among urban groups, distinct from armed cadres
GS3 · Ideology and extremism
The debate on 'urban Naxals' shows the line the state must hold between countering extremism and protecting dissent.
Last-mile connectivity
Roads and mobile towers reaching remote forest villages
GS3 · Infrastructure and security
Mobile towers in Bastar are last-mile connectivity that also serves as last-mile security.
data: LWE-affected districts: early 2000s, end of 2025, MHA review of February 2026
Government data cited by The Indian Express
LWE-affected districts fell from about 200 in the early 2000s to just seven in February 2026.
Fall in LWE-related incidents and resultant deaths since 2010
Government data cited by The Indian Express
LWE incidents and deaths have fallen by over four-fifths since 2010.
examples: 76 CRPF jawans killed, the peak of LWE
Dantewada 2010: 76 CRPF jawans killed, the peak of LWE.
Eklavya schools in Bastar: classrooms as counter-insurgency.
Mobile towers in forests: connectivity as security.
pyqs: Determinants of LWE in eastern India.
Does tribal development policy reflect equity-based governance?
Threats from external state and non-state actors.

trend.t: LWE questions moved from causes (non-implementation of the Fifth Schedule, 2013; determinants in eastern India, 2020) to LWE as a development issue (2022) and then to the government's elimination target and measures (2025). Tribal development reappeared in 2026 as a question of equity-based governance.
trend.watch: LWE has been asked in 2013, 2020, 2022 and 2025, and the 2025 question was about the elimination target itself, so the 'after Naxalism' phase is the next likely angle: consolidation, development and rehabilitation in freed areas.
focus: Security plus development strategy and its results
Fifth Schedule, PESA and Forest Rights Act in freed areas
Rehabilitation of surrendered cadres and victims
Ideological contest: countering extremism while protecting dissent

potential: "Defeating armed insurgency is only half the task; winning the trust of the people is the other half." Discuss with reference to Left Wing Extremism in India. (15 marks)
Examine the role of infrastructure and welfare delivery in containing Left Wing Extremism. (10 marks)
What should be India's strategy to consolidate peace in areas freed from Left Wing Extremism? (15 marks)

practice.q: "Defeating armed insurgency is only half the task; winning the trust of the people is the other half." Discuss with reference to Left Wing Extremism in India.
parts: How the armed threat was defeated
Why trust is the other half

answer.t: LWE-affected districts fell from nearly 200 in the early 2000s to seven in February 2026, yet the PM warned in Bastar that the ideological danger 'has not completely disappeared'.

answer.h: How the armed threat was defeated

pts.t: Security forces were given the freedom to take every necessary decision, with sustained operations in core areas.
pts.ex: No CRPF jawan lost his life on duty over the past year, a first in 47 years.

pts.t: Support that LWE received from sympathisers within the system was targeted alongside armed cadres.
pts.ex: The PM's reference to stopping support from 'people sitting within the system'.

pts.t: Roads and mobile towers opened up the forests to forces and to the state.
pts.ex: Mobile towers and roads in Bastar.

pts.t: Eklavya schools and ITIs brought services into areas once cut off.
pts.ex: Eklavya model residential schools in tribal districts.

pts.t: Joint operations and shared intelligence across the Red Corridor states.
pts.ex: The MHA's periodic district-wise review of LWE affected areas.

pts.t: A time-bound goal created focus and accountability.
pts.ex: The March 31, 2026 'Naxal-free' target announced in the Lok Sabha.

answer.h: Why trust is the other half

pts.t: LWE grew from land alienation, displacement and a governance deficit; these do not end with operations.
pts.ex: Non-implementation of the Fifth Schedule was asked by UPSC in 2013.

pts.t: Unsettled forest rights and displacement for mining can revive grievance.
pts.ex: Forest Rights Act and PESA implementation gaps.

pts.t: Naxalites 'snatched away the right to vote'; elections and gram sabhas must now carry people's voice.
pts.ex: Strong turnout in former LWE areas as a test of trust.

pts.t: An ideology is countered by delivering justice and opportunity, not by force alone.
pts.ex: The PM's call to 'identify' intellectual Naxals.

pts.t: Countering extremist ideology must not chill legitimate criticism and tribal rights activism.
pts.ex: Article 19 freedoms and due process.

pts.t: Surrendered cadres and victims need livelihoods, or the cycle restarts.
pts.ex: Surrender-cum-rehabilitation policies of states.

pts.t: Shift from security camps to schools, health centres and banks in freed areas.
pts.ex: ITIs and Eklavya schools in Bastar.

pts.t: Implement PESA and the Forest Rights Act in letter and spirit.
pts.ex: Gram sabha consent for land and forest use.

pts.t: Skilling and local jobs to absorb young people.
pts.ex: Minor forest produce value chains.

pts.t: Community policing and grievance redress to build confidence.
pts.ex: Civic action programmes of the CAPFs.

pts.t: Tribal languages and culture respected in schools and administration.
pts.ex: Mother-tongue primary education.

pts.t: Keep the district-wise review going to prevent a relapse.
pts.ex: MHA's 'LWE affected' categorisation.

answer.t: The guns have largely fallen silent; India now has to make the state as present in a Bastar village's daily life as the security camp once was.

title: Meet the Siddis: Tribal Gujaratis from Kathiawad, natural athletes of African stock
syllabus: GS1 › Salient features of Indian society; diversity · GS2 › Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections (Scheduled Tribes, PVTGs) · GS4 › Inclusive governance; equity; compassion towards the weaker sections
summary: Khushbu Darjada, 15, became the first Siddi athlete to win a Youth Olympics medal (judo silver); the Siddis of Gujarat, of African descent, are a PVTG of about 12,959 people.
ideas: Siddis: African-origin, Gujarati-speaking PVTG; Sufi-Hindu blend.
GS1 · Diversity
India's syncretic diversity.
ST in Saurashtra, SEBC elsewhere: protection by geography.
GS2 · ST classification
Inconsistent status fragments rights.
Sport and education as ladders, if support continues.
GS2 · Vulnerable sections / GS4 · Equity
Inclusion needs follow-through.
keywords: PVTG
Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, marked by small, stagnant population and low development
GS2 · Tribal welfare
The Siddis are among 75 PVTGs who need targeted, culturally sensitive development.
Equity vs equality
Equity gives extra support to those who start behind; equality treats all alike
GS4 · Inclusive governance
Sports quotas and coaching for Siddi youth are equity, not favour.
Syncretism
Blending of different religious and cultural traditions
GS1 · Indian society
Siddi rituals that mix Sufi Islam and Hindu practice are an example of Indian syncretism.
examples: GS2 · Vulnerable sections · GS4 · Inclusive governance

first Siddi woman to clear Gujarat PSC
Afsana Makwa: first Siddi woman to clear Gujarat PSC.

When diverse tribes can be treated as one category.
Legal initiatives against discrimination of STs.

trend.t: Tribal questions moved from constitutional basis (2016) and discrimination (2017) to whether diverse tribes can be one category (2022), displacement (2025) and, in 2026, whether tribal policy reflects equity-based governance.

focus: Sport and education as ladders of mobility

potential: "Inclusive governance is measured by the opportunities it creates at the margins." Discuss with reference to Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups. (10 marks)

title: Flagship fest ahead, why Nagaland wants permit regime scrapped
syllabus: GS3 › Security challenges and their management in border areas; Linkages of development and security · GS2 › Federalism and Centre–state relations; Issues relating to the Northeast · GS1 › Tribal culture · GS4 › Citizen-friendly administration
summary: Nagaland has urged the Centre to completely withdraw the Protected Area Permit for foreigners, reimposed in December 2024 for security reasons, saying it hurts tourism ahead of the Hornbill Festival.
ideas: Two permits, two purposes: the PAP (Foreigners (Protected Areas) Order, 1958) controls foreigners' entry to border states, while the colonial-era ILP regulates Indian citizens to protect indigenous hill cultures.
GS3 · Border management / GS1 · Tribal culture
India's permit regimes serve two aims: security at the border (PAP) and protection of tribal cultures (ILP).
Security versus development: relaxed in 2011 and reimposed in December 2024 for security reasons, the PAP now clashes with the state's push for tourism and investment.
GS3 · Linkages of security and development
In peaceful border states, rigid security rules can choke the development that itself secures the region.
A rule from another era: the CM argues that a regulation designed for a different security environment should not hold back a peaceful state's aspirations.
GS2 · Governance / Policy review
Rules must be reviewed as conditions change; regulations that outlive their purpose become obstacles.
Process matters as much as policy: bureaucracy, a convoluted application process and last-minute relaxations deter foreign tourists who plan months ahead.
GS2 · Governance / GS4 · Citizen-friendly administration
Predictable, simple procedures matter as much as the rule itself for tourism and trust.
Federal voice: the state wants a central rule changed and has taken it to the Union Home Minister, but awaits a decision.
GS2 · Federalism
Nagaland's appeal on the PAP shows states seeking a voice in central rules that shape their development.
keywords: Protected Area Permit (PAP)
Central permit for foreigners to visit designated border areas
GS3 · Border management
The PAP balances border security against openness to foreign visitors.
Inner Line Permit (ILP)
Permit for Indian citizens to enter certain northeastern states
GS1 · Tribal protection / GS2
The ILP protects indigenous cultures from demographic and economic pressures.
Security–development nexus
The idea that development and security reinforce each other
GS3 · Internal security
In the Northeast, tourism-led development can strengthen peace as much as security controls.
Regulatory sunset
Reviewing or ending a rule once its purpose has passed
GS2 · Governance
A sunset review would test whether the PAP still serves security in peaceful states.
Cultural tourism
Tourism built on a region's living culture and festivals
GS1 · Culture / GS3 · Economy
Festivals like Hornbill turn culture into livelihoods and soft power.
examples: Flagship festival drawing visitors from across the world
GS1 · Culture · GS3 · Tourism · Act East
The Hornbill Festival is an example of the Northeast's cultural soft power and tourism potential.
Security rule swinging with the security assessment
The PAP's relaxation and reimposition show security policy shifting with threat perceptions.
Relaxation announced only around the festival gives tourists no certainty
A relaxation that comes too late to plan for is an example of form over substance in administration.
pyqs: Internal security challenges and peace accords in the North-Eastern States.
Security challenges in policing the border in North-East India beyond insurgency.
Border Area Development Programmes and civic action in Ladakh.
Challenges and strategies for effective border management.
Hill states reaching the limits of ecological carrying capacity due to tourism.

trend.t: Northeast questions moved from insurgency and border policing (2017, 2019) to peace accords (2025), while border questions shifted in 2026 to development programmes that win hearts and minds. The direction is from security alone to security through development.
trend.watch: The Northeast and border management are asked almost every year. Prepare the balance of security and development, peace processes and border-area development.
focus: Security and development in border areas
Northeast: peace processes and special arrangements
Permit regimes (PAP, ILP) and tribal protection
Tourism and the Act East policy

potential: "In India's border states, development is itself a security strategy." Discuss with reference to the Northeast. (15 marks)
Distinguish between the Inner Line Permit and the Protected Area Permit. Should the PAP be relaxed in peaceful northeastern states? (10 marks)
Examine the potential of cultural tourism in the economic development of the Northeast. (10 marks)

practice.q: "In India's border states, development is itself a security strategy." Discuss with reference to the Northeast.

answer.t: In November 2026 Nagaland asked the Centre to withdraw the Protected Area Permit, reimposed in 2024, arguing that a rule from another security era holds back a peaceful state's development.

pts.t: Livelihoods cut the pool of youth drawn to insurgency.
Visitors bring income and integrate the region with the world.
pts.ex: Hornbill Festival draws visitors from many countries.

pts.t: Roads, rail and air links bind border areas to the mainland.
pts.ex: Act East connectivity projects.

pts.t: Schools, health and services build trust in government.
Thriving villages deter infiltration better than empty borders.
pts.ex: Vibrant Villages Programme.

pts.t: Development sustains peace accords.
pts.ex: Peace accords in the Northeast in the past decade.

pts.t: Movement of insurgents, arms and drugs across international borders.
Instability in Myanmar affects the region.
Proximity to China calls for caution on foreign access.
The ILP shields indigenous identity from outside pressure.
Relax the PAP where conditions are peaceful, with safeguards.
Online, time-bound approvals that foreigners can plan for.
Involve states in decisions on central rules that shape their economies.
Technology at borders so that security does not depend on blanket restrictions.
Tourism, crafts and agro-processing for local youth.
Community-led tourism that respects indigenous ways of life.

answer.t: In the Northeast, a confident state secures its borders by opening its doors with care; balancing permits with prosperity is the surest path to lasting peace.
